name: Cornelius Vanderbilt
wealthNote: His estate was about $105M in 1877, which Wikipedia equates to roughly $3.17B in 2025 dollars. The tier uses that inflation-adjusted figure.
humbleBeginnings: Born on Staten Island in 1794, he quit school at 11 to work on his father's ferry. At 16 he borrowed $100 from his mother to buy a periauger, a small sailing boat, and ran his own ferry between Staten Island and Manhattan.
breakthrough: Moved into steamboats working for Thomas Gibbons, whose Gibbons v. Ogden victory (1824) broke a state steamboat monopoly. During the Gold Rush he set up the Accessory Transit Company across Nicaragua. From the 1860s he took control of the Harlem, Hudson River and New York Central railroads and merged them in 1869.
shieldingStrategy: Consolidated his railroads into one corporation, the New York Central & Hudson River Railroad, and built Grand Central Depot (1871) to anchor it. He then left about 95% of his estate to his son William Henry so the empire would not be split, a choice the other heirs challenged in a will contest.

breakthroughDetail.d: At 16 he used $100 borrowed from his mother to start a Staten Island–Manhattan ferry, which earned him the nickname 'the Commodore'.

He set up the Accessory Transit Company with others to carry Gold Rush passengers across Nicaragua. After filibuster William Walker seized its Nicaraguan assets in 1855, forces backed by Vanderbilt ousted Walker in 1857.
He took control of the New York & Harlem (1863), the Hudson River Railroad (1864) and the New York Central (1867), and merged the Central with the Hudson River line on November 1, 1869.
His 1868 attempt to corner Erie Railway stock failed after Daniel Drew, Jay Gould and James Fisk issued unauthorized shares.

shieldingDetail.d: He merged his lines into the New York Central & Hudson River Railroad and built Grand Central Depot (1871), so the system ran as a single company.

shieldingDetail.t: Kept the fortune in one pair of hands.
shieldingDetail.d: He left about 95% of his ~$105M estate to William Henry Vanderbilt, and the other heirs contested the will.
In 1873 he gave $1M, then the largest charitable gift in U.S. history, to found what became Vanderbilt University in Nashville.
Wall Street broker Jeremiah G. Hamilton clashed with him over control of the Accessory Transit Company in the 1850s.

name: Andrew Carnegie
wealthNote: His personal share of the 1901 sale to J.P. Morgan was about $225.6M in 5% gold bonds. He gave away about $350M in his lifetime, which Wikipedia equates to $6.9B in 2025 dollars. No single modern net-worth figure is published, so the tier is an inflation-adjusted estimate.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835, he came to Allegheny, Pennsylvania, at 12 in 1848. His first job was as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill for $1.20 a week, followed by work as a telegraph messenger.
breakthrough: Joined the Pennsylvania Railroad under Thomas A. Scott in 1853 and became superintendent of its Western Division in 1859, investing early in sleeping cars, oil and the Keystone Bridge Company. He then built a Bessemer steel empire (Edgar Thomson Works, Homestead) that became Carnegie Steel in 1892 and sold it to J.P. Morgan in 1901.
shieldingStrategy: Kept Carnegie Steel a closely held partnership in which he held a controlling stake. An 'iron clad' partnership agreement let the firm buy out departing partners at book value. After the sale he set out to give the fortune away, as in his 'Gospel of Wealth' (1889), and put the remaining $135M into Carnegie Corporation of New York (1911).

breakthroughDetail.d: He started under Thomas A. Scott at the Pennsylvania Railroad in 1853 and was made superintendent of the Western Division on December 1, 1859.
He put $500 into Adams Express (1855), took shares in Woodruff's sleeping-car company, invested in Columbia Oil (1864) and ran Keystone Bridge, which supplied steel for the Eads Bridge.
He named the Edgar Thomson Steel Works after his old railroad boss, bought Homestead in 1883 and formed Carnegie Steel on July 1, 1892, with Frick, Lauder and Phipps.
He sold to J.P. Morgan in March 1901 and personally received about $226M, mostly in 5% 50-year gold bonds of the new U.S. Steel.

shieldingDetail.d: The agreement let the firm buy out a departing partner at book value. In 1899 Carnegie used it to force out Henry Clay Frick, who sued; Frick settled for shares worth over $30M in the reorganized company.
As controlling shareholder of a private partnership, he could not be removed, and the firm reported to no public shareholders.
Taking gold bonds rather than U.S. Steel shares gave him a fixed income and left him out of the new company's management.

'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.' He funded 2,509 libraries (1,679 in the U.S.), Carnegie Technical Schools (1900) and Carnegie Corporation of New York (1911, $135M), and served as a Cornell trustee from 1890 to 1919.

name: Elon Musk

X.com merged with Confinity to form PayPal, and eBay bought PayPal for $1.5B in 2002, paying him about $175.8M. He put that money into SpaceX (2002) and led Tesla's 2004 Series A.

At SpaceX's 2026 IPO his super-voting shares carried over 80% of the votes, and Tesla moved its incorporation from Delaware to Texas in 2024. He signed the Giving Pledge in 2012, and the Musk Foundation held over $14B by the end of 2024.

breakthroughDetail.d: Compaq paid $307M in cash for Zip2 in February 1999, and Musk got $22M for his 7%. eBay's $1.5B purchase of PayPal in 2002 paid him about $175.8M for his 11.72%.
He founded SpaceX in 2002 with about $100M of his own money. In February 2004 he put $6.5M of Tesla's $7.5M Series A into the company and became its chairman. In 2008 he also became Tesla's CEO.
In January 2015 Google and Fidelity invested $1B in SpaceX for just under 10%, and Google's Don Harrison joined SpaceX's board. Alphabet disclosed a roughly 6% stake worth $94.1B after the 2026 IPO.

After a Delaware court threw out his $56B Tesla pay package, Tesla reincorporated in Texas (June 2024). In November 2025 shareholders approved a new performance award worth up to $1T over 10 years.

He joined the Giving Pledge in April 2012, in the same announced group as John Sall and Sequoia's Michael Moritz. In 2021 he gave about $5.7B of Tesla shares to charity, the same period as his roughly $16B of share sales. The Musk Foundation held over $14B at the end of 2024.
He took Twitter private on Oct 27, 2022 for about $44B, then merged it into xAI and xAI into SpaceX, so the assets moved between companies he controls.

name: Larry Page
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1973 in Lansing, Michigan. His father was a computer science professor at Michigan State and his mother taught programming there. He studied computer engineering at Michigan (1995) and started a PhD at Stanford, where he met Sergey Brin.

Google listed on Aug 19, 2004 at $85 a share and raised about $1.67B. Page became CEO again in 2011, made Google part of the Alphabet holding company in 2015, and stepped down as CEO in December 2019.
He and Brin invested in Tesla's $40M third round in May 2006. Google later put money into Musk's SpaceX in 2015.

The Carl Victor Page Memorial Foundation, named for his father, held over $1B in assets as of 2013.

Since 2005 his wealth has been run by a private family office, Bayshore Global Management, which also has an office in Singapore. In December 2025 he dissolved or moved about 15 California LLCs, several of them to Nevada.

breakthroughDetail.d: His family arrived in the U.S. on Oct 25, 1979. His father became a mathematics professor and his mother a NASA researcher. He finished Maryland in 1993 and earned a Stanford MS in 1995.
He co-developed PageRank with Page, and the company started in Susan Wojcicki's Menlo Park garage. Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia led the $25M 1999 round, and the 2004 IPO raised about $1.67B.

He co-founded Bayshore Global Management with Anne Wojcicki in 2005, after the IPO. It manages about $100B in direct investments and real estate plus the Sergey Brin Family Foundation, and opened a Singapore office in late 2020.

breakthroughDetail.d: Loopt was in Y Combinator's first batch in 2005, raised more than $30M (Sequoia and NEA led the Series A) and sold to Green Dot for $43.4M in March 2012. Altman succeeded Paul Graham as YC president in February 2014.

breakthroughDetail.d: OpenAI launched in December 2015 with Musk and Altman as co-chairs and $1B pledged by backers including Thiel and AWS. Altman became CEO in 2019, and ChatGPT launched in November 2022.
The board removed him on November 17, 2023. Microsoft's Satya Nadella said he would join Microsoft, more than 700 of 770 staff threatened to follow, and he was reinstated on November 21.

Hydrazine Capital, co-founded with his brother in 2012, raised a $21M first fund with Thiel as main backer and put most of it into YC companies. Its later funds hold stakes he can diversify across hundreds of companies.
He stepped down as chairman of nuclear startup Oklo in April 2025 to avoid conflicts with OpenAI.
Signed with husband Oliver Mulherin in May 2024, committing most of his wealth to philanthropy.

name: Dario Amodei
humbleBeginnings: Born in San Francisco in 1983 to an Italian-American leather craftsman and a Jewish-American librarian. He studied physics at Caltech and Stanford and earned a Princeton PhD in biophysics in 2011.
breakthrough: After research jobs at Baidu and Google, he joined OpenAI in 2016 and rose to VP of Research, working on GPT-2, GPT-3 and RLHF. He left with six colleagues to found Anthropic in 2021, which private investors valued at $965B in May 2026.
shieldingStrategy: Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation whose Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock and elects a growing share of the board. His wealth is a roughly 2% founder stake (Forbes estimate), and he says all seven co-founders have pledged to donate 80% of their wealth.

breakthroughDetail.d: Princeton biophysics PhD and Stanford Medicine postdoc, then Baidu (2014–15) and Google before joining OpenAI in 2016.

breakthroughDetail.t: Built the scaling playbook at OpenAI.
breakthroughDetail.d: As VP of Research he worked on GPT-2 and GPT-3 and co-invented reinforcement learning from human feedback (Forbes).
Co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with six other ex-OpenAI staff, including his sister Daniela as president.

Amazon ($8B) and Google ($3B+) invested from 2023, and Microsoft and Nvidia committed up to $15B in November 2025. The valuation reached $965B in May 2026, and Anthropic filed confidential IPO papers in June 2026.

shieldingDetail.d: As a Delaware PBC, directors may legally weigh the public-benefit purpose against shareholder returns.
An independent trust holds special Class T stock and elects a rising number of directors, reaching a board majority within four years of the Series C.
"All of Anthropic's co-founders have pledged to donate 80% of our wealth" (The Adolescence of Technology, January 2026). Staff pledges are matched by the company.
Forbes estimates each of the seven co-founders owns about 2%, so no single founder holds outright control.

name: Daniela Amodei
humbleBeginnings: Born in San Francisco in 1987 and went to Lowell High School. She studied English literature at UC Santa Cruz on a classical flute scholarship, then worked in global health and as a communications manager for Rep. Matt Cartwright.
breakthrough: Joined Stripe as an early employee in 2013 and moved to OpenAI in 2018, where she managed teams during GPT-2 and later led safety and policy. In 2021 she co-founded Anthropic with her brother Dario and became its president.
shieldingStrategy: Her wealth is an estimated 2% founder stake in Anthropic, a Delaware public benefit corporation governed partly by its Long-Term Benefit Trust. She is one of the seven co-founders who pledged to donate 80% of their wealth.

breakthroughDetail.d: Moved from global health and congressional politics to Stripe as an early employee in 2013.
Joined OpenAI in 2018, managed teams during GPT-2's development and then led safety and policy work.

breakthroughDetail.t: Runs the business side of Anthropic.
breakthroughDetail.d: As president since the 2021 founding, she leads the company alongside CEO Dario. Forbes valued each co-founder's stake at $15.5B after the May 2026 round.

shieldingDetail.d: Anthropic's Delaware PBC status and the Long-Term Benefit Trust's Class T stock limit how far ordinary shareholders, founders included, can steer the board.
Covered by the co-founders' pledge to donate 80% of their wealth, announced in January 2026.
She is married to Holden Karnofsky, co-founder of the grantmaker Open Philanthropy.

name: Alex Karp
humbleBeginnings: Born in New York in 1967 to a Jewish pediatrician and an African-American artist, and raised in Philadelphia. He studied philosophy at Haverford, earned a JD at Stanford Law (where he met Thiel) and a PhD in social theory in Frankfurt.
breakthrough: Started the London money manager Caedmon Group with a $12,000 inheritance, then co-founded Palantir with Thiel and three others in 2003 and became CEO. Palantir direct-listed in 2020 and joined the S&P 500 in 2024.
shieldingStrategy: Palantir's Class F shares, held in a founders' voting trust by Karp, Thiel and Stephen Cohen, carry 49.999999% of the votes regardless of how many shares the founders own. A direct listing let insiders sell without a traditional IPO lock-up.

breakthroughDetail.d: Ran Caedmon Group in London for European high-net-worth investors, seeded with a $12,000 inheritance from his grandfather.
Palantir was founded on May 6, 2003. Thiel's fund largely bankrolled the first $30M, and In-Q-Tel put in about $2M.
Listed on the NYSE on September 30, 2020, joined the S&P 500 in September 2024 and moved to Nasdaq in November 2024. Revenue was $4.48B in 2025.
In November 2024 Palantir, Anthropic and AWS agreed to bring Claude to U.S. defense and intelligence agencies through Palantir's AI platform.

shieldingDetail.d: Class F stock keeps the founders' bloc at 49.999999% of voting power as long as they hold a minimum number of Class B shares. Any two of the three founders direct the trust.
Palantir left Palo Alto for Denver in 2020 and announced a move to the Miami area in February 2026.
He lives in Lyman, New Hampshire and is reported to have relocated to Liechtenstein, where he is building a home.

name: Peter Thiel
humbleBeginnings: Born in Frankfurt in 1967, he moved to Cleveland as a baby and spent 1971–77 in South Africa and Namibia before settling in Foster City, California. He studied philosophy at Stanford, co-founded The Stanford Review and earned a Stanford JD in 1992.
breakthrough: Left law and derivatives trading to co-found PayPal in 1998. It merged with Musk's X.com in 2000 and sold to eBay for $1.5B in 2002. He then made the first outside investment in Facebook ($500K in 2004), co-founded Palantir (2003) and Founders Fund (2005).
shieldingStrategy: ProPublica reported, from IRS records, that he grew a Roth IRA from under $2,000 in 1999 to more than $5B by 2019 by buying founder-priced PayPal shares and other early stakes inside it, so the gains can come out tax-free. He also holds founders' voting control at Palantir and gained New Zealand citizenship in 2011.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded with Max Levchin and Luke Nosek in 1998. After the 2000 merger with Musk's X.com it sold to eBay in 2002, and Thiel's 3.7% stake was worth about $55M.
Paid $500,000 for 10.2% in August 2004, joined the board and stayed until February 2022. He has since sold most of the stake.
Incorporated Palantir in May 2003 with Karp and others; his fund largely bankrolled its first $30M. He chairs the company.
Started in 2005 with Ken Howery and Nosek. It was the first institutional investor in SpaceX and Palantir, and it co-led Anthropic's $30B Series G in February 2026.

shieldingDetail.d: Bought 1.7M PayPal founder shares at $0.001 each inside a Roth IRA in 1999. ProPublica reported the account held more than $5B by 2019, tax-free if left until age 59½.
Holds Palantir Class F voting power with Karp and Cohen, which is fixed at 49.999999% of votes.
Invests through Thiel Capital (1996), Founders Fund, Valar Ventures (2010) and Mithril Capital (2012) instead of a single fund.
Granted New Zealand citizenship in 2011, in addition to U.S. and German citizenship.

name: Warren Buffett
humbleBeginnings: Born in Omaha in 1930, the son of a stockbroker who became a U.S. congressman. He was not poor, but he made his own early money from paper routes, pinball machines and selling used cars, bought his first stock at 11, and studied under Benjamin Graham at Columbia.
breakthrough: After working at Graham-Newman he started Buffett Partnership Ltd. in 1956. He did not found Berkshire Hathaway: he bought shares in the failing New Bedford textile mill from 1962, fell out with its manager Seabury Stanton over a tender price, and bought control by 1965. He then turned it into a holding company for insurance float, whole businesses and big stock stakes such as Coca-Cola (1988).
shieldingStrategy: Nearly all his wealth sits in Berkshire stock, which keeps its earnings instead of paying them out, so he has realized little taxable income. He gives the shares away in annual gifts: about $48B to the Gates Foundation from 2006, and since 2026 only to his children's four foundations. The rest is set to pass through a charitable trust run by his three children.

breakthroughDetail.d: He began buying Berkshire Hathaway shares in 1962 expecting a liquidation profit. When Stanton offered less than promised in a tender, Buffett bought control (1965) and fired him. He later called it his biggest investment mistake.
Berkshire used insurance cash to buy whole companies (Geico, Dairy Queen, Duracell) and large stakes. It bought 7% of Coca-Cola for $1.02B in 1988 and still holds about 9%.

In 2008 Berkshire put $5B into Goldman Sachs preferred stock paying 10% (Goldman bought it back for $5.5B in 2011) and $3B into GE preferred. In 2011 it bought $5B of Bank of America preferred with warrants, which it turned into 700M common shares in 2017.
Greg Abel succeeded him as CEO on January 1, 2026. On September 18, 2026 his son Howard Buffett replaced him as chairman, and Warren became chairman emeritus.

shieldingDetail.d: Berkshire keeps its earnings inside the company instead of paying them out, so his fortune grows as unrealized gains on stock he has never sold.
In 2006 he pledged about 10 million Berkshire B shares to the Gates Foundation over his lifetime. The foundation received about $48B in all. He served as a trustee until June 2021.

His July 2026 gift of about $6B in Berkshire shares left out the Gates Foundation for the first time in 20 years. It went to the Susan Thompson Buffett, Howard G. Buffett, Sherwood and NoVo foundations instead.
He launched the Giving Pledge with Bill Gates in 2010 and has committed more than 99% of his wealth to philanthropy.

name: Stephen A. Schwarzman
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in the Philadelphia suburbs, where his father owned a dry-goods store. At 14 he started a lawn-mowing business, finding the clients while his younger twin brothers did the mowing. He went on to Yale and Harvard Business School.
breakthrough: He ran mergers and acquisitions at Lehman Brothers, then left in 1985 to co-found Blackstone with his former Lehman boss Peter Peterson, with $400,000 of their own money. Blackstone grew from an M&A boutique into the world's largest alternative-asset manager, with about $1.3 trillion under management by 2026.
shieldingStrategy: His fortune is his Blackstone stake and his share of the fees and carried interest it earns. He took the firm public in 2007 but stayed chairman and CEO. He has tied his name to large institutional gifts and signed the Giving Pledge in 2020.

breakthroughDetail.d: Peterson and Schwarzman, both from Lehman, founded Blackstone in 1985 with $400,000 of seed capital. The name joins 'Schwarz' (black) and 'Peter' (stone).

In 1987 Blackstone backed Larry Fink's bond team in a 50-50 venture that became BlackRock. Blackstone sold its stake to PNC for $240M in the mid-1990s, which Schwarzman later called his worst business decision.
Blackstone bought Hilton Hotels for about $26B including debt in 2007, took it public again in 2013 and was fully out by 2018, with roughly $14B of profit.
Blackstone joined KKR, Goldman Sachs and others in the $11.3B SunGard buyout (2005).

shieldingDetail.d: The June 2007 IPO sold a 12.3% stake for $4.13B. Schwarzman stayed chairman and CEO, with Jonathan Gray as president.
In 2025 his total compensation from Blackstone was about $1.24B.
His gifts include $100M to the New York Public Library, $100M for Schwarzman Scholars at Tsinghua, $350M to MIT for a computing college, $150M to Yale and £150M to Oxford.
He signed the Giving Pledge in 2020.

name: Henry Kravis
humbleBeginnings: Not humble: born in Tulsa in 1944, the son of Raymond Kravis, a successful oil engineer who had been a business partner of Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. He went to Loomis Chaffee, Claremont McKenna and Columbia Business School.
breakthrough: At Bear Stearns he, his cousin George Roberts and their boss Jerome Kohlberg did early 'bootstrap' buyouts of family companies. They left in 1976 to found Kohlberg Kravis Roberts. The firm's debt-financed buyouts of Beatrice (1986) and RJR Nabisco (1989, about $25B, financed with Drexel junk bonds) defined the 1980s LBO era.
shieldingStrategy: He has held control through KKR's partnership structure. Even after KKR listed (2010) and became a corporation, KKR Management LLP, owned by him and Roberts, kept control. A 2021 reorganization ends that control on the 'Sunset Date' (no later than December 31, 2026). His wealth also funds named gifts to Columbia, Memorial Sloan Kettering and Loomis Chaffee.

breakthroughDetail.d: Kohlberg, Kravis and Roberts did leveraged deals at Bear Stearns, including Orkin Exterminating (1964), before going independent in 1976.

KKR bought Beatrice in 1986 and sold it off in pieces. Its international food arm went to Reginald Lewis for $985M in 1987. Black Enterprise reports that Kravis doubted Lewis's credibility until Michael Milken vouched for him.

KKR won RJR Nabisco at $109 a share against a management bid backed by Shearson Lehman Hutton. At about $25B ($31B including debt) it was the largest LBO in history. Drexel Burnham Lambert raised about $5B of the financing as junk bonds.
KKR led the $44B TXU buyout (2007) with TPG and Goldman Sachs, and joined Blackstone and others in the 2005 SunGard deal.

shieldingDetail.d: Under the October 2021 Reorganization Agreement, KKR Management LLP's control through Series I Preferred Stock ends on the Sunset Date, after which voting becomes one vote per share.
In 2021 he and Roberts handed the co-CEO roles to Joe Bae and Scott Nuttall but stayed on as executive co-chairmen.

He has given $100M to Columbia Business School (2010) plus $25M (2015), $100M to Memorial Sloan Kettering (2022) and $100M to Loomis Chaffee (2024). His wife Marie-Josée Kravis chairs the board of MoMA.

name: George R. Roberts
humbleBeginnings: Born in Houston in 1943 into a well-off family. He went to Culver Military Academy, Claremont McKenna College (1966) and UC Hastings law school, then joined his cousin Henry Kravis at Bear Stearns, where he made partner at 29.
breakthrough: He co-founded KKR in 1976 with Kravis and Jerome Kohlberg. By 1978 KKR had raised its first institutional fund. Together they made the leveraged buyout an institutional asset class, from Beatrice and Safeway (1986) to RJR Nabisco.
shieldingStrategy: He shares the founders' control of KKR through KKR Management LLP, which ends on the 2021 agreement's Sunset Date (no later than December 31, 2026). He is executive co-chairman. His giving goes mainly through REDF, the employment social-enterprise fund he founded, and to Claremont McKenna.

breakthroughDetail.d: At Bear Stearns the future KKR partners did early leveraged acquisitions such as Orkin Exterminating (1964).
By 1978 KKR had raised its first institutional fund with outside investor commitments.
KKR's $5.5B Safeway buyout (1986) was a friendly deal that helped management fend off hostile bidders.
He co-led the 1988–89 RJR Nabisco buyout, the largest LBO of its era, which became the subject of 'Barbarians at the Gate.'

shieldingDetail.d: Under the October 2021 Reorganization Agreement, KKR Management LLP's Series I control ends on the earlier of December 31, 2026, or six months after both founders have died or become disabled.
He founded REDF (Roberts Enterprise Development Fund), which funds businesses that employ people facing barriers to work.
He gave Claremont McKenna $50M in 2012 and $140M in 2022.

name: Marc Rowan
humbleBeginnings: Born on Long Island in 1962 and raised in Hollywood, Florida. His father worked in auto leasing and his mother was a teacher. After his father died, the University of Pennsylvania let him finish at Wharton despite the family's financial hardship. He earned a BS and an MBA there.
breakthrough: He joined Drexel Burnham Lambert's M&A group in 1985. When Drexel collapsed in 1990, he co-founded Apollo with fellow Drexel bankers Leon Black and Josh Harris. Apollo bought the distressed debt of failed insurers and S&Ls and converted it into control. Rowan built its insurance engine, Athene, after 2008, became CEO in 2021, and saw Apollo pass $1 trillion in assets in 2026.
shieldingStrategy: His wealth is his Apollo stake. The three founders together kept about 58% of Apollo after its 2011 IPO. Separately, he owns Hamptons and North Fork restaurants through Montauk Asset Holdings. His philanthropy runs through Penn (a $50M Wharton gift in 2018) and UJA-Federation of New York, which he chairs.

breakthroughDetail.d: Rowan, Black and Harris met in Drexel's M&A department and founded Apollo in 1990, after the junk-bond house went bankrupt.
Apollo's first big trade, alongside Credit Lyonnais, was buying the junk-bond portfolio of the seized Executive Life Insurance Company.
Apollo and TPG bought Harrah's Entertainment in 2008 for about $27.8B including debt. Rowan joined the board when the deal closed, and Harrah's was later renamed Caesars.
He helped found the annuity company Athene after 2008. Apollo bought it outright in an $11B all-stock deal in January 2022, one of his first major deals as CEO.

shieldingDetail.d: Apollo listed on the NYSE in 2011, with the three co-founders holding 58%, and joined the S&P 500 in December 2024.
He owns Hamptons-area restaurants, including Duryea's Lobster Deck, through Montauk Asset Holdings.
His $50M gift to Wharton (2018) was the school's largest at the time, and he chaired Wharton's board of advisors until 2025.

name: Charles Schwab
humbleBeginnings: Born in Sacramento in 1937, the son of a lawyer who served as a district attorney. He grew up in Woodland and Santa Barbara, sold ice cream and caddied as a boy, and got through Stanford while struggling with dyslexia, which wasn't diagnosed until he was about 40.
breakthrough: He started First Commander Corp. in San Francisco in 1971, with $100,000 borrowed from an uncle, and renamed it Charles Schwab & Co. in 1973. After the SEC deregulated commissions in 1975, he cut his prices roughly in half and paid brokers salaries instead of commissions. That turned Schwab into the leading discount broker, which later bought TD Ameritrade (2020).
shieldingStrategy: He sold the company to Bank of America in 1983 for $55M and bought it back in 1987, so he kept founder control and the later gains. He still owns about 6% of the public company and is chairman. He moved his residence to Florida after selling his San Francisco home in 2020.

breakthroughDetail.d: When the SEC ended fixed brokerage commissions, Schwab halved his prices, paid salaries instead of commissions and added toll-free, round-the-clock phone trading.
Bank of America bought Schwab in 1983 for $55M. Management, led by Schwab, bought it back in 1987, and he took it public that year.
Schwab bought U.S. Trust for $2.73B (2000) and sold it to Bank of America for $3.3B (2007), then bought TD Ameritrade in 2020.

shieldingDetail.d: He still holds about 6% of the Charles Schwab Corporation and stayed chairman after stepping down as CEO in 2008.
Repurchasing the firm from Bank of America before the 1987 IPO put the later growth in his hands rather than the bank's.
After learning of his own dyslexia through his son's diagnosis, he became a backer of research and support for children with learning differences.

name: Thomas Peterffy
humbleBeginnings: Born in Budapest in 1944, during a Soviet air raid. He reached New York in 1965 with almost nothing and worked as an architectural draftsman, then as a computer programmer, including at the commodities trader Mocatta Metals.
breakthrough: In 1977 he bought an American Stock Exchange seat for about $36,000 and traded options as a market maker using his own pricing models. His firm Timber Hill brought handheld computers onto the trading floor in the early 1980s. In 1993 he spun its technology out as Interactive Brokers, a low-cost electronic broker that went public in 2007.
shieldingStrategy: He controls Interactive Brokers through IBG Holdings LLC, which held about 73.5% of the operating company in 2026, while the listed shares hold the rest. The 2007 IPO floated only 10%. He also owns more than 560,000 acres of land, mostly in Florida.

breakthroughDetail.d: He saved about $200,000 as an engineer-programmer and in 1977 bought an AMEX seat for $36,000 to trade options.
T.P. & Co. became Timber Hill in 1982 and introduced handheld computers to trading floors in the early 1980s.
Interactive Brokers was incorporated in 1993 to offer Timber Hill's execution technology to customers. It went public on Nasdaq in May 2007 by selling 10% in a Dutch auction.
In 2020 Interactive Brokers took over Folio Investments' retail business from Goldman Sachs.

shieldingDetail.d: IBG Holdings LLC held 73.5% of IBG LLC's membership interests and about 73.7% of the voting power in 2026, while public shareholders held 26.5%.
Forbes counts him among the largest landowners in the U.S., with more than 560,000 acres, mostly in Florida.
He handed the CEO role to Milan Galik in 2019 and remains chairman and the controlling shareholder.

name: Carl Icahn
humbleBeginnings: Born in Brooklyn in 1936 and raised in Far Rockaway, Queens. His father was a cantor and substitute teacher and his mother a schoolteacher. He studied philosophy at Princeton (1957), briefly attended NYU medical school, and served in the Army Reserve before becoming a stockbroker at Dreyfus in 1961.
breakthrough: In 1968 he bought a New York Stock Exchange seat with $150,000 of his own money and $400,000 from an uncle. From Tappan (1978) onward he bought stakes in undervalued companies and forced sales or buybacks. Drexel's 'highly confident' letter, first written for his Phillips Petroleum raid, gave him a way to finance threatened takeovers. TWA (1985), Texaco, USX and RJR Nabisco followed, and later Netflix, Apple, Dell and eBay.
shieldingStrategy: He holds about 86% of Icahn Enterprises, a publicly traded master limited partnership that holds his businesses, and stopped managing outside money in 2011. A 2023 Hindenburg short report showed he had pledged much of his stake for personal loans, and in 2024 he paid a $500,000 SEC penalty over that disclosure without admitting wrongdoing.

breakthroughDetail.d: Drexel first used the letter in Icahn's attempt on Phillips Petroleum. Leon Black, later an Apollo founder, was the lead banker. Icahn didn't win control but sold his shares back at a profit.

He took 50% of Trans World Airlines in 1985 and bought the rest in a 1988 LBO, then sold assets such as its London routes ($445M to American, 1991). Wikipedia says he made $469M and left TWA with $540M of debt.

He announced a bid for USX (U.S. Steel) on October 6, 1986, and dropped it in early 1987. From 1995 to 2000, at first alongside Bennett LeBow, he ran four proxy fights to force RJR Nabisco to split off its food business.
He took a 10% Netflix stake in 2012, campaigned for Apple buybacks in 2013–14, sued to derail Michael Dell's $24.4B buyout in 2013, and pushed eBay to spin off PayPal in 2014.

shieldingDetail.d: Icahn Enterprises (formerly American Real Estate Partners) is a Nasdaq-listed limited partnership, about 86% owned by him, that holds energy, auto, food-packaging and real-estate businesses.

In 2024 the SEC fined Icahn Enterprises $1.5M and Icahn $500,000 for not disclosing that his units were pledged for personal loans. Neither admitted wrongdoing. The partnership halved its distribution in August 2023.
He signed the Giving Pledge in 2010 and has given about $200M to Mount Sinai, whose medical school now bears his name.

name: Phil Knight
peakWealth: $24.4B (Forbes real-time, Oct 5 2026); Wikipedia cites $35.4B as of October 2025
humbleBeginnings: Born in Portland, Oregon in 1938, he ran track at the University of Oregon under coach Bill Bowerman (B.B.A. 1959). At Stanford's business school (MBA 1962) he wrote a paper asking whether Japanese running shoes could do to German shoes what Japanese cameras had done to German cameras. After graduating he sold Japanese running shoes from the trunk of his car.
breakthrough: In 1962 he found Onitsuka Tiger shoes in Kobe and became their U.S. distributor. On Jan 25, 1964 he and Bowerman each put in $500 to start Blue Ribbon Sports, which became Nike in 1971. Nike went public in December 1980, by which time it had about half the U.S. athletic-shoe market, and FY2025 revenue was $46.3B.
shieldingStrategy: Control runs through Nike's two share classes: Class A elects three-quarters of the board. Knight moved his Class A shares into Swoosh, LLC in 2015 and sold its voting units to a trust of his son Travis in 2016. He gives through the Knight Foundation and large gifts to Stanford, Oregon and OHSU.

breakthroughDetail.d: Blue Ribbon Sports started in Eugene as a distributor for Onitsuka Tiger, funded with $500 each from Knight and Bowerman on a handshake, then launched its own Nike brand in 1971.
He commissioned the Swoosh from designer Carolyn Davidson for $35 in 1971 and later gave her a few hundred shares when the company went public.
Nike listed in December 1980 with about 50% of the U.S. athletic-shoe market. It bought Converse for $309M in 2003 and was #90 on the 2025 Fortune 500.

shieldingDetail.t: Class A shares elect most of the board.
shieldingDetail.d: Nike's Class A holders elect three-fourths of the directors, so the founder's block keeps control even though most traded stock is Class B.

Knight put his Class A stock (257M shares after the 2015 split) into Swoosh, LLC. On June 30, 2016 he sold its voting units to an entity of the Travis A. Knight 2009 Irrevocable Trust II and left Nike's board, so control passed to his son without breaking up the block.

Forbes counts $4.5B given, mainly through the Knight Foundation, including $105M (2006) to Stanford GSB, $400M (2016) for Knight-Hennessy Scholars, over $2B to Oregon and a $2B pledge (2025) to OHSU's Knight Cancer Institute.

name: Ralph Lauren
humbleBeginnings: Born Ralph Lifshitz in the Bronx in 1939 to Jewish immigrant parents, he worked as a teenage stock boy and changed his surname to Lauren at 16. After Army service he sold at Brooks Brothers and then sold ties for Beau Brummell.
breakthrough: In 1967, at 28, he talked Beau Brummell's president into letting him launch his own line of ties, working from a single drawer in the Empire State Building. Neiman Marcus ordered 1,200 ties, the Polo menswear line followed in 1968 and women's wear in 1971. The company listed on the NYSE on June 12, 1997.
shieldingStrategy: He kept voting control through high-vote Class B stock, which Forbes puts at 85% of the votes. He sold 28% of the company to a Goldman Sachs fund in 1994 for $135M and floated it in 1997, taking cash out while keeping control. He stepped down as CEO in 2015 but stayed executive chairman and chief creative officer.

breakthroughDetail.d: He started with men's ties in 1967; a 1,200-tie order from Neiman Marcus put the brand into department stores.
Menswear under the Polo name (1968), women's wear (1971), the costumes for The Great Gatsby (1974), fragrances (1978) and the Rhinelander mansion flagship (1986) widened it into a lifestyle label.
Licensees such as Reed & Barton and WestPoint Stevens made Home Collection products under the brand, extending it without the company building every factory.

shieldingDetail.d: In 1994 he sold 28% to a Goldman Sachs investment fund for $135M. His stake was worth over $400M after the 1997 listing.
Forbes reports he controls 85% of the voting rights, so outside holders cannot replace him.
His son David is chief branding and innovation officer, and Lauren remains executive chairman and chief creative officer after giving up the CEO role in 2015.
He owns the 17,000-acre Double RL ranch in Colorado (bought from 1982) and a car collection valued at over $600M.

name: Brian Chesky
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1981 in Niskayuna, New York, the son of two social workers. He studied industrial design at the Rhode Island School of Design (BFA 2004) and was earning about $40,000 a year as a designer when he moved to San Francisco in 2007.
breakthrough: In October 2007 he and RISD classmate Joe Gebbia rented air mattresses in their apartment during a design conference; Nathan Blecharczyk joined as technical co-founder. They kept going by selling 'Obama O's' and 'Cap'n McCain's' cereal boxes, got $20,000 from Y Combinator in early 2009 and $600,000 from Sequoia that April. Airbnb listed on Nasdaq on Dec 10, 2020, raising $3.5B.
shieldingStrategy: Airbnb's dual-class shares give him about 11% of the economics and roughly a third of the votes. He signed the Giving Pledge in 2016 and in 2022 pledged $100M with the Obamas for the Voyager Scholarship.

breakthroughDetail.d: Election-themed cereal boxes raised about $20,000–$30,000 to pay the founders' debts before outside money arrived.

Y Combinator's Winter 2009 batch gave $20,000 for 6%. Sequoia put in $600,000 of seed in April 2009, and joined Greylock in the $7.2M Series A (November 2010). Founders Fund led a $200M round in 2012.
In April 2020 Silver Lake and Sixth Street provided $1B of equity and $1B of debt at 9%–11.5%. Eight months later the IPO raised $3.5B, and Sequoia's $375M of investments were worth about $15B.

shieldingDetail.d: Wikipedia gives his stake as 10.7% economic and 31.9% voting, so the three founders together keep effective control.
He joined the Giving Pledge in 2016, and in 2022 pledged $100M to the Obama Foundation's Voyager Scholarship.
Sam Altman credited Chesky and Ron Conway with steadying him during his November 2023 removal from OpenAI; Chesky publicly backed him and advised him through his return.

name: Tony Xu
humbleBeginnings: Born in Nanjing, China around 1984, he came to the U.S. as a small child and grew up in Champaign, Illinois. His mother, a doctor in China, worked as a server in a Chinese restaurant before opening acupuncture clinics. He studied industrial engineering at UC Berkeley and worked at PayPal, eBay, McKinsey and Square before Stanford's business school (MBA 2013).
breakthrough: With Stanford classmates Andy Fang, Stanley Tang and Evan Moore he ran PaloAltoDelivery.com (2012), which became DoorDash in January 2013. Y Combinator gave $120,000 for 7% that summer, and Sequoia led a $17.3M Series A in 2014. The December 9, 2020 IPO raised $3.37B, and DoorDash later bought Wolt (€7B, 2021) and Deliveroo ($3.9B, 2025).
shieldingStrategy: He owns about 4.6% of DoorDash but held voting authority over all Class B shares, about 69% of the votes at the IPO. He and his wife Patti signed the Giving Pledge.

breakthroughDetail.d: PaloAltoDelivery.com (2012) tested whether local restaurants wanted delivery; it became DoorDash in January 2013.
Sequoia's Alfred Lin initially passed, then led the $17.3M Series A in May 2014 and joined the board. Sequoia invested $415M in total, worth over $8.5B after the IPO.
DoorDash bought Caviar from Square for $410M (2019), Wolt for €7B (2021) and Deliveroo for $3.9B (2025).

shieldingDetail.d: Company proxies record that from October 1999 he took an annual salary of $1 'to demonstrate his belief in the company's long term viability'.
He rolled his stake into the 2007 take-private and kept a large share of the company it became, so his wealth is mostly KMI stock rather than pay.
He and his wife Nancy started the Kinder Foundation in 1997. It has committed more than $850M, mostly in Houston. They are also Giving Pledge signers.

name: Harold Hamm
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1945 in Lexington, Oklahoma, the 13th and youngest child of cotton sharecroppers. He started working at a gas station at 16 and then took oil-refinery work. Before drilling, he ran a trucking business hauling water for oilfields.
breakthrough: Founded Shelly Dean Oil in 1967, named for his two daughters, and renamed it Continental Resources in 1990. Continental found the Cedar Hills field in North Dakota in 1995. In 2004 it completed the first commercially successful horizontal, fracked well in the North Dakota Bakken, a key step in the US shale boom.
shieldingStrategy: Took Continental public in 2007, then in November 2022 his family bought out the public shareholders for $4.3B in cash. The company is now 100% owned by the Harold Hamm Family LLC. He is a Giving Pledge signer.

breakthroughDetail.d: Started with a single company in 1967, borrowed to drill his own wells, and grew without an outside sponsor.
Discovered North Dakota's Cedar Hills field, described as the 7th-largest onshore field in the lower 48 states by liquid proved reserves.
In 2004 Continental drilled the first commercially successful horizontally drilled and fracked well in the North Dakota Bakken.
At the 2007 IPO Hamm sold about $300M of shares and kept control.

shieldingDetail.d: In November 2022, Hamm family affiliates acquired the shares they did not already own for about $4.3B, so Continental no longer reports to public shareholders.
Continental is now held 100% by the Harold Hamm Family LLC, and Forbes notes that ownership was distributed among family members in the buyout.
His 2014 divorce from Sue Ann Arnall ended with a payment of about $975M, one of the largest settlements on record.
He has signed the Giving Pledge and funded the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma.

name: Leonard Schleifer
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1953 in Queens, the son of a sweater manufacturer who had been a WWII codebreaker. He went to Cornell on scholarship, then earned an MD-PhD at the University of Virginia under future Nobel laureate Alfred Gilman. He was teaching at Weill Cornell when he started the company.
breakthrough: Co-founded Regeneron in 1988 with scientist George Yancopoulos, starting with $1 million of seed money from Merrill Lynch venture capitalist George Sing. He took it public in 1991. Eylea (approved 2011) and Dupixent (2017) became blockbusters, and Regeneron now has 12 FDA-approved medicines.
shieldingStrategy: Has run Regeneron since founding and controls it through its pre-IPO Class A stock, which carries ten votes per share. His wealth is his stake of about 2% of the common stock. Partnerships, mainly with Sanofi and later BARDA, paid for much of the research so the founders were not heavily diluted.

breakthroughDetail.d: Schleifer, a neurologist teaching at Cornell, recruited Yancopoulos, and the two have run the company together since 1988.
Eylea (aflibercept), approved in November 2011 for age-related macular degeneration, made Schleifer a billionaire. It brought in $4.8B in US sales in 2024.
Sanofi took a stake in 2007 and funded collaborative development. In 2020 Regeneron bought back about 19.2M of Sanofi's shares for around $5B.
Under a 2017 BARDA agreement the US government funded 80% of development for some antibody drugs, and that platform later produced the REGEN-COV COVID-19 antibodies.

shieldingDetail.d: Regeneron's 2025 proxy says Class A stock carries ten votes per share and none has been issued since the 1991 IPO. Schleifer holds most of the roughly 1.8M Class A shares outstanding.
His 2014 compensation of about $42M, the highest among biopharma CEOs that year, came mostly in stock awards, which built his ownership.
Using Sanofi and BARDA money for R&D meant fewer new shares had to be sold, preserving the founders' stakes.

name: Alan B. Miller
wealthNote: Forbes does not list him. The 2025 UHS proxy shows him beneficially owning about 8.0M shares across Classes A, B and C (5.16M Class A, 0.66M Class C, and Class B including conversions), worth about $1.4B at $175.72 (Oct 2, 2026). Part of this is held in LLCs and 2024 GRATs for his children, so his personal share may be lower. Tiered conservatively at $500M-$1B because part of the ~8.0M beneficially owned UHS shares sits in his children's trusts and LLCs.
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1937 in Brooklyn to immigrant parents. His father owned a dry-cleaning store and his mother worked for a millinery company. He studied at William & Mary and earned a Wharton MBA.
breakthrough: In 1973 he took over struggling hospital chain American Medicorp and turned it around, but lost it to a hostile takeover by Humana in 1978. In April 1979 he founded Universal Health Services with six employees and no revenue. UHS owned four hospitals within 18 months, went public in 1981, and became a Fortune 500 hospital and behavioral-health operator, helped by the $3.1B Psychiatric Solutions deal in 2010.
shieldingStrategy: Built a multi-class share structure: he holds all of the Class C stock (100 votes per share) and about 78% of Class A, which gives him about 88% of UHS's voting power while owning a small part of its equity. In 2021 he handed the CEO role to his son Marc and became executive chairman.

breakthroughDetail.d: His American Medicorp turnaround earned industry recognition but ended when Humana won a hostile bid in 1978, which pushed him to start a company he could control.
Within 18 months of its 1979 founding UHS owned four hospitals and managed two more. It listed in 1981 and joined the S&P 500 in 2014.
The $3.1B purchase of Psychiatric Solutions (2010), followed by Cygnet in the UK and other deals, made UHS a major behavioral-health operator with more than 300 facilities.

shieldingDetail.d: Each Class C share carries 100 votes. In the 2025 proxy Miller held all 661,688 Class C shares and 78.5% of Class A, for 87.8% of the general voting power.
Some of his shares are held through three LLCs and three 2024 grantor retained annuity trusts (GRATs) for his children.
His son Marc D. Miller became CEO in January 2021, and Alan stayed on as executive chairman.
In 2020 UHS agreed to a $122M settlement with the DOJ over billing for medically unnecessary behavioral-health services from 2006 to 2018.

name: John Malone
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1941 in Milford, Connecticut. He earned degrees from Yale, Johns Hopkins (including a PhD in operations research) and NYU, then worked in economic planning at Bell Labs, at McKinsey, and running General Instrument's Jerrold Electronics unit. He started out as an engineer-economist, not a man of inherited wealth.
breakthrough: Bob Magness hired him at Tele-Communications Inc. (TCI), and he became CEO in 1973 at 32. By 1982 he had made it the largest US cable company through debt-financed acquisitions. He spun off Liberty Media in 1991, and in 1999 sold TCI to AT&T for $32B in stock plus $16B of assumed debt.
shieldingStrategy: Known as the 'Cable Cowboy', he used tax-free spinoffs, tracking stocks and asset swaps instead of taxable sales. Super-voting Class B shares keep him in control across Liberty Media, Liberty Global and their spinoffs. He also holds about 2 million acres of land.

breakthroughDetail.d: TCI grew through acquisitions such as United Artists Entertainment (1991) and carried about $15B of debt by the mid-1990s, using cash flow rather than reported earnings as the measure.
Comcast and the TCI spinoff Liberty Media bought QVC together in February 1995. Liberty bought out Comcast's 56.5% in 2003 for $7.9B.
AT&T agreed to buy TCI in June 1998 and closed in March 1999. TCI's systems became AT&T Broadband, which Comcast bought in 2002.
An $11B swap with News Corp in 2008 gave Liberty 47.9% of DirecTV, Charlie Ergen's main rival. In 2013 Malone publicly urged that DISH and DirecTV merge.

shieldingDetail.d: Liberty has spun off Liberty Global, Discovery, Starz, Liberty Broadband, the Atlanta Braves (2023) and SiriusXM (2024) instead of selling them in taxable deals.
Liberty issues stocks that track separate asset groups, such as Formula One, under one corporate parent.
Malone keeps voting control of Liberty Media through its Class B shares despite repeated restructurings.

shieldingDetail.t: Land as a store of value.
shieldingDetail.d: He was the largest private landowner in the US from 2011 to 2021, with about 2.2 million acres in Maine, Colorado, New Mexico and Wyoming.

name: Charlie Ergen
humbleBeginnings: Born in 1953 in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the son of an Austrian nuclear physicist. He earned a Wake Forest MBA and worked as a financial analyst at Frito-Lay, then quit in 1978 and played poker and blackjack professionally for a time.
breakthrough: In 1980 he, his future wife Candy and Jim DeFranco put $60,000 into EchoSphere and sold C-band satellite dishes from a truck around Denver. EchoStar went public and launched its first satellite in 1995, and the DISH Network brand followed in 1996. DISH was spun off in 2008, and the two were recombined under EchoStar at the end of 2023.
shieldingStrategy: Controls EchoStar as its 'controlling shareholder' through Class B shares carrying ten votes each, about 90% of the voting power. He spent about a decade buying wireless spectrum and sold much of it in 2025 for cash and SpaceX stock. He and Candy are Giving Pledge signers.

breakthroughDetail.d: EchoSphere began in 1980 with $60,000 and sold satellite antennas door to door around Denver.
EchoStar I launched on December 28, 1995, and the DISH Network brand followed on March 4, 1996, moving the company from selling hardware to selling subscriptions.
In the late 1990s News Corp's planned tie-up with EchoStar fell apart. Ergen later said 'Malone got what he wanted' from that episode. Malone's Liberty went on to hold 47.9% of rival DirecTV.
In 2025 EchoStar agreed to sell spectrum to AT&T for $23B and to SpaceX for about $17B, half of it in SpaceX stock.

shieldingDetail.d: Each EchoStar Class B share carries ten votes, and Ergen is the company's controlling shareholder with roughly 90% of the voting power.
Cantey (Candy) Ergen, a co-founder in 1980, serves as a director and senior advisor.

shieldingDetail.t: Spectrum as a store of value.
shieldingDetail.d: Licenses bought over about a decade were later sold for roughly $40B, turning a declining pay-TV business into cash and SpaceX equity.
'Candy and Charlie Ergen' appear on the Giving Pledge list.

name: Tyrone D. Taborn
wealthNote: No published net-worth figure, and this is a low-confidence estimate at the bottom of the tier. It rests on his roughly 40 years of private ownership of Career Communications Group, which business-data aggregators estimate at about $4-7M in annual revenue and HistoryMakers calls a 'multimillion-dollar' company, plus the BEYA conference franchise. No sale, valuation or real-estate figure is public.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Los Angeles in an African American and Latino household (HistoryMakers gives his birth as Chicago, 1959). He graduated from Cornell, where he was a Telluride Association scholar, also holds a BS from Johns Hopkins, and in 1978 was the first LBJ Congressional Intern, in Rep. Julian Dixon's office.
breakthrough: In the mid-1980s (company materials give both 1985 and 1986) he founded Career Communications Group in Baltimore to publish US Black Engineer, later US Black Engineer & Information Technology. With Morgan State engineering dean Eugene DeLoatch he co-founded the Black Engineer of the Year Awards, first held at Morgan State in February 1987. BEYA grew into a STEM conference with 100+ recruiting companies and more than 10,000 attendees.
shieldingStrategy: Kept CCG private and diversified it from one magazine into a set of titles (Hispanic Engineer, Women of Color) and events, sponsored by corporations and defense contractors. He plans to step down as publisher in 2028 and become board chairman, and family member Ty Oliver Taborn is general counsel.

breakthroughDetail.d: US Black Engineer profiled Black engineers and technologists whose work was 'too often missing from mainstream publications'. CCG has digitized back issues to 1984.
The first Black Engineer of the Year Awards were held at Morgan State in February 1987, during National Engineers Week, with Dr. John Slaughter as the first honoree.

BEYA is co-hosted by CCG, the Council of Engineering Deans of the HBCUs, and Lockheed Martin, which by 2011 had co-hosted for more than a decade. Boeing, Raytheon, Northrop Grumman and IBM also recruit there.
An early report to Mobil's CEO led him to write to other Fortune 500 heads endorsing the program, which helped bring in corporate sponsors.

shieldingDetail.d: CCG has stayed privately held under Taborn since its founding and publishes no financials.
Revenue comes from several magazines and conferences, BEYA and the Women of Color STEM Conference, plus digital platforms such as STEM City USA, rather than a single title.
Taborn will step down as publisher in 2028 and remain chairman of the board while a new publisher is recruited.
In 2025 Taborn said some government agencies and corporate employers were reconsidering BEYA participation amid the backlash against DEI programs.

description: Ron Burkle's Los Angeles buyout firm, founded 1986. It owned 70% of Golden State Foods from 1998 until 2004.

name: Wetterau Inc.
description: St. Louis family food distributor founded in 1869 and sold to SuperValu for $1.1B in 1992. The sale funded Wetterau Associates.

name: Marfrig
description: Brazilian meatpacker that bought Keystone Foods for $1.26B (2010), sold its distribution arm to Martin-Brower (2012), and sold the rest to Tyson (2018).

name: Tyson Foods
description: U.S. meat company that bought Keystone Foods from Marfrig in 2018 for $2.16B, beating bids from Cargill and others.

name: Ronald McDonald House Charities
description: McDonald's-linked children's charity, a recurring civic tie among the chain's suppliers.

name: Epic Systems
description: Electronic health record vendor founded in Madison in 1979 (as Human Services Computing), now in Verona, WI. Never VC-funded, never acquisitive, never public, and locked private by a voting trust.

name: PeopleSoft
description: HR/ERP software company founded in 1987 by Dave Duffield and Ken Morris. Acquired by Oracle in January 2005 for about $10.3–10.7B after an 18-month hostile takeover fight.

name: Workday
description: Cloud HR and finance software company founded in 2005 by PeopleSoft's Duffield and Bhusri and headquartered in Pleasanton, PeopleSoft's old home town. Public since 2012 with founder dual-class control.

name: Oracle
description: Database and applications giant whose 2003–2005 hostile takeover of PeopleSoft prompted the founding of Workday.

name: Trilogy
description: Austin software company founded by Joe Liemandt in 1989 on credit-card debt. Still private, it owns Versata and others and spun off the Aurea roll-up.

name: ESW Capital
description: Joe Liemandt's private buyer of mature software companies (more than 100 per Forbes), run for maintenance cash flow with Crossover contractors.

name: Alpha School
description: Austin-founded (2014) school built on two-hour AI-tutored academic days, funded by about $1B from Joe Liemandt.

name: Esri
description: Redlands, CA mapping-software company founded in 1969 by Jack and Laura Dangermond. Privately owned with no debt or outside investors, it holds about 40% of the GIS market.

name: Vista Equity Partners
description: Austin-based enterprise-software buyout firm founded in 2000 by Robert F. Smith, with about $100B under management.

name: Reynolds and Reynolds
description: Dealership-management software company taken private in 2006 by Robert Brockman's Universal Computer Systems for about $2.8B.

name: Barr Systems
description: Gainesville, FL print/output-management software firm founded in 1983 by SAS co-founder Anthony Barr.

name: Cary Academy
description: Private school in Cary, NC, founded in 1996 by Jim and Ann Goodnight and John and Ginger Sall. SAS supports it through a scholarship program.

name: The Giving Pledge
description: Commitment by the very wealthy to give away the majority of their wealth. Signers in this cluster include the Salls, Faulkner, the Dangermonds, Smith and the Bhusris.

name: The Nature Conservancy
description: U.S. conservation group. John Sall sat on its board (2002–2011), and the Dangermonds gave its largest-ever gift, $165M in 2017.

name: University of Wisconsin–Madison
description: Where Judy Faulkner earned her computer science master's. Epic started in Madison.

name: Goldman Sachs
description: Wall Street bank where Robert F. Smith and Brian Sheth both worked in technology M&A before Vista.

name: Greylock Partners
description: Silicon Valley VC firm. Aneel Bhusri has been a partner since 1999, and it co-funded Workday.

name: Maddie's Fund
description: Animal-welfare foundation endowed with $200M by Dave and Cheryl Duffield in 1994 and named for their schnauzer.

name: Morehouse College
description: Atlanta men's college whose 2019 graduating class had its student debt (~$34M) paid off by Robert F. Smith.

name: JPMorgan Chase
description: Traces to Drexel, Morgan & Co. (1871), renamed J.P. Morgan & Co. in 1895. It merged with Chase Manhattan on December 1, 2000.

name: Morgan Stanley
description: Founded September 16, 1935, by Henry S. Morgan (J.P. Morgan's grandson) and Harold Stanley after Glass-Steagall forced J.P. Morgan & Co. to choose commercial banking.

name: U.S. Steel
description: Formed by J.P. Morgan in 1901 from Carnegie Steel, Federal Steel and National Steel; the first billion-dollar corporation. Since June 18, 2025, it has been a wholly owned subsidiary of Nippon Steel, delisted from the NYSE, with a U.S. government golden share.

name: Carnegie Steel Company
description: Andrew Carnegie's steel partnership, formed July 1, 1892, with Frick, Lauder and Phipps. Morgan bought it in 1901 and it ran as a U.S. Steel subsidiary under the same name for 35 years.

name: General Electric
description: Formed April 15, 1892, when J.P. Morgan merged Edison General Electric and Thomson-Houston. After the 2023–24 breakup its legal successor is GE Aerospace, whose official GICS sub-industry is used here.

name: New York Central Railroad
description: Vanderbilt took control in 1867 and merged it with the Hudson River Railroad in 1869. In 1879 Morgan sold a large block of William H. Vanderbilt's shares and joined its board. It merged into Penn Central in 1968.

name: Pennsylvania Railroad
description: Where Andrew Carnegie rose from telegrapher to division superintendent under Thomas A. Scott. In 1885 Morgan brokered its truce with the New York Central over the West Shore and South Pennsylvania lines.

name: Northern Securities Company
description: Holding company formed in 1901 by J.P. Morgan, James J. Hill and E.H. Harriman for the Great Northern, Northern Pacific and Burlington railroads. The Supreme Court ordered it dissolved under the Sherman Act on March 14, 1904.

name: Vanderbilt University
description: Founded in Nashville in 1873 with Cornelius Vanderbilt's $1M gift, then the largest charitable gift in U.S. history.

name: Carnegie Corporation of New York
description: Founded by Andrew Carnegie in 1911 with $135M. It was renamed the Andrew Carnegie Foundation on June 9, 2026, and its endowment is about $5B.

name: Carnegie Mellon University
description: Founded by Andrew Carnegie in 1900 as the Carnegie Technical Schools in Pittsburgh. It merged with the Mellon Institute in 1967.

name: Google (Alphabet)
description: Founded by Page and Brin in 1998 and part of Alphabet since 2015. Class B shares carry 10 votes, which keeps the founders in control. It invested in SpaceX in 2015 and held about 6% after the 2026 IPO.

name: Tesla
description: Founded in 2003 by Eberhard and Tarpenning. Musk led its 2004 Series A, and Page and Brin invested in 2006. Goldman Sachs co-led its 2010 IPO, and it moved its incorporation to Texas in 2024.

name: SpaceX
description: Founded by Musk in 2002. Google and Fidelity invested $1B in 2015. It bought xAI in February 2026 and listed on Nasdaq (SPCX) on June 12, 2026, with Musk keeping super-voting control.

name: xAI
description: Musk's AI company, announced in July 2023. It absorbed X Corp in March 2025 and became a SpaceX subsidiary in February 2026. Grok 2 was trained on Oracle cloud GPUs.

name: X (Twitter)
description: Twitter, which Musk took private on Oct 27, 2022 for about $44B. It was merged into xAI in March 2025.

name: PayPal
description: Formed in 2000 when Musk's X.com merged with Confinity. eBay bought it for $1.5B in 2002. It is now an S&P 500 company.

name: eBay
description: Bought PayPal for $1.5B in 2002, which gave Musk about $175.8M.

name: Zip2
description: Web software firm co-founded in 1995 by Elon and Kimbal Musk and Greg Kouri. Compaq bought it for $307M in cash in 1999.

name: OpenAI
description: Founded in December 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk co-founded it partly as a counterweight to Google's AI work, and Isaacson reports it ended his friendship with Larry Page.

name: Fidelity Investments
description: Privately held fund firm that co-led SpaceX's $1B round with Google in January 2015.

name: Kleiner Perkins
description: Co-led Google's $25M round in June 1999. Partner John Doerr sits on Alphabet's board.

name: Sequoia Capital
description: Co-led Google's $25M round in June 1999. Partner Michael Moritz joined the Giving Pledge in 2012, in the same group as Musk and John Sall.

name: Bayshore Global Management
description: Sergey Brin's family office, founded in 2005 and based in Palo Alto with a Singapore office. It manages about $100B and the Sergey Brin Family Foundation.

name: Koop
description: Larry Page's private family office. It has no website and was reincorporated in Delaware in December 2025.

name: Musk Foundation
description: Musk's foundation, which received a large gift of Tesla shares in 2021 and held over $14B in assets at the end of 2024.

name: Anthropic
description: Founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI staff led by Dario and Daniela Amodei. It is a Delaware public benefit corporation overseen partly by a Long-Term Benefit Trust. It was valued at $965B in May 2026 and filed confidential IPO papers in June 2026. Tagged Application Software as the closest fit, because it sells Claude subscriptions and API access, matching how openai and xai are tagged.

name: Palantir Technologies
description: Founded May 6, 2003 by Thiel, Karp, Stephen Cohen, Joe Lonsdale and Nathan Gettings, with early money from Thiel and the CIA's In-Q-Tel. It direct-listed in 2020, joined the S&P 500 in 2024, and its Class F shares give the founders 49.999999% of the vote.

name: Founders Fund
description: San Francisco VC firm started in 2005 by Thiel, Ken Howery and Luke Nosek, with about $17B under management in 2025. It was the first institutional investor in SpaceX and Palantir and an early Facebook investor.

name: Y Combinator
description: Founded in March 2005 by Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris and Trevor Blackwell, and has funded more than 5,000 startups. Its alumni include Loopt (first batch), Airbnb, Stripe and Reddit.

name: Loopt
description: Mobile geosocial app co-founded in 2005 by Sam Altman, Nick Sivo and Alok Deshpande. Sequoia and NEA led its Series A, and Green Dot bought it for $43.4M in March 2012.

name: Hydrazine Capital
description: Venture firm Sam and Jack Altman co-founded in 2012. Its first fund raised $21M with Peter Thiel as the main backer and invested mostly in YC companies.

name: Stripe
description: Private payments company and Y Combinator alumnus. Daniela Amodei joined in 2013 as an early employee, Sam Altman is an early investor, and Founders Fund holds a stake. It was valued at $159B in February 2026 (Forbes). Tagged by its closest listed peers.

name: Amazon
description: Jeff Bezos's company, #2 on the 2025 Fortune 500. It invested $8B in Anthropic in 2023–24, and AWS was one of the backers that pledged $1B to OpenAI at its 2015 founding.

name: Microsoft
description: Co-founded by Bill Gates in 1975 and #14 on the 2025 Fortune 500. It invested in OpenAI from 2019 and held about 27% after OpenAI's 2025 restructuring. In November 2025 it committed up to $5B to Anthropic.

name: Nvidia
description: Co-founded by Jensen Huang in 1993 and #31 on the 2025 Fortune 500. In September 2025 it signed a letter of intent to supply OpenAI with 10GW of systems and invest up to $100B, and in November 2025 it committed up to $10B to Anthropic.

name: Meta Platforms (Facebook)
description: Facebook, founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004 and #22 on the 2025 Fortune 500. Peter Thiel made its first outside investment ($500K for 10.2%) in 2004 and sat on its board until 2022.

name: Berkshire Hathaway
description: Former New Bedford textile maker that Buffett took control of in 1965 and turned into an insurance-funded conglomerate (Geico, Duracell, Dairy Queen) with large stakes in Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola and Bank of America. Greg Abel became CEO in 2026.

name: Blackstone
description: Founded in 1985 by Peter Peterson and Stephen Schwarzman with $400,000. Now the world's largest alternative-asset manager (about $1.3T), spanning buyouts, real estate and credit. Public since 2007.

name: KKR
description: Kohlberg Kravis Roberts, founded in 1976 by ex-Bear Stearns bankers Jerome Kohlberg, Henry Kravis and George Roberts. It made the leveraged buyout famous with Beatrice and RJR Nabisco. Listed on the NYSE in 2010 and joined the S&P 500 in 2024.

name: Apollo Global Management
description: Founded in 1990 by Drexel Burnham Lambert alumni Leon Black, Josh Harris and Marc Rowan. Built on distressed-to-control investing and Athene's retirement annuities, it passed $1T in assets in 2026.

name: Charles Schwab Corporation
description: Discount brokerage founded in San Francisco in 1971 (as First Commander, renamed 1973). Owned by Bank of America from 1983 to 1987, public since 1987, and bought TD Ameritrade in 2020.

name: Interactive Brokers
description: Electronic broker that grew out of Thomas Peterffy's market maker Timber Hill. Public since 2007 but controlled by Peterffy, and added to the S&P 500 in August 2025.

name: Icahn Enterprises
description: Nasdaq-listed master limited partnership (formerly American Real Estate Partners), about 86% owned by Carl Icahn, holding energy (CVR), automotive, food packaging and real-estate businesses.

name: RJR Nabisco
description: Its 1988–89 buyout by KKR for about $25B (about $31B including debt), partly financed with Drexel junk bonds, was the largest LBO in history until the mid-2000s. Carl Icahn later fought to split it. Its tobacco and food businesses were separated in 1999.

name: Beatrice Foods
description: Chicago food conglomerate bought by KKR in 1986 and broken up. Its international arm was sold to Reginald Lewis's TLC Group in 1987 for $985M, and the rest went to ConAgra in 1990.

name: Caesars Entertainment
description: Casino company (formerly Harrah's). Apollo and TPG took it private in 2008 for about $27.8B, and Carl Icahn's 2019 stake and board seats pushed it into the Eldorado merger.

name: Trans World Airlines (TWA)
description: U.S. airline that Carl Icahn took control of in 1985 and bought outright in a 1988 LBO, selling off assets such as its London routes.

name: Hilton Worldwide
description: Hotel company that Blackstone bought for about $26B (including debt) in 2007, took public again in 2013 and fully exited in 2018 with about $14B of profit.

name: Bank of America
description: Owned Charles Schwab's brokerage from 1983 to 1987. Berkshire Hathaway's 2011 $5B preferred investment became one of its largest stakes.

name: Apple
description: iPhone and Mac maker and one of Berkshire Hathaway's largest stock holdings. Carl Icahn held a stake from 2013 to 2016 and campaigned for buybacks.

name: Lehman Brothers
description: Wall Street bank where Stephen Schwarzman ran M&A and Peter Peterson had worked before they founded Blackstone in 1985. It collapsed in 2008.

name: Bear Stearns
description: Investment bank where Jerome Kohlberg, Henry Kravis and George Roberts did early bootstrap buyouts before leaving to form KKR in 1976. Sold to JPMorgan Chase in 2008.

name: Gates Foundation
description: Bill Gates's foundation, plans to close by 2045. Warren Buffett gave it about $48B in Berkshire stock from 2006 and was a trustee until 2021, but stopped giving to it in 2026.

name: Columbia University
description: New York university. Buffett earned his economics master's at Columbia Business School under Benjamin Graham, and Henry Kravis (MBA 1969) gave the business school $100M.

name: Claremont McKenna College
description: Liberal-arts college in California and alma mater of both KKR cousins. George Roberts gave it $190M across 2012 and 2022.

name: University of Pennsylvania
description: Home of the Wharton School, where Marc Rowan earned his BS and MBA and gave $50M (2018), and where Warren Buffett studied from 1947 to 1949.

name: Nike
description: Founded as Blue Ribbon Sports on Jan 25, 1964 by Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman; renamed Nike in 1971 and listed in 1980. Class A shares, held through Swoosh, LLC, elect three-quarters of the board. Ariel's John Rogers Jr. was a director from 2018 to 2026.

name: Ralph Lauren Corporation
description: Started in 1967 with men's ties; listed on the NYSE on June 12, 1997. A Goldman Sachs fund bought 28% for $135M in 1994. Ranked #537 on Fortune's 2025 list, so it is outside the Fortune 500.

name: Airbnb
description: Founded in 2008 by Chesky, Gebbia and Blecharczyk. Backed by Y Combinator (2009), Sequoia, Greylock and Founders Fund; IPO Dec 10, 2020 raised $3.5B. Sequoia's Alfred Lin joined its board in 2012.

name: DoorDash
description: Founded in 2013 by Stanford students. Sequoia led its $17.3M Series A in 2014 and Alfred Lin joined the board, so it shares a Sequoia board member with Airbnb. It bought Caviar from Square (2019), Wolt (2021) and Deliveroo (2025).

name: Carvana
description: Started in 2012 inside DriveTime and listed in April 2017. It sells its auto loans to Ally under a forward-flow agreement, restructured its bonds with Apollo-led holders in 2023 and joined the S&P 500 on Dec 22, 2025.

name: DriveTime
description: Ernest Garcia II bought the bankrupt Ugly Duckling rent-a-car franchise in 1991, listed it in 1996 and took it private in 2002 as DriveTime. Its affiliate Bridgecrest services loans. It funded Carvana's start.

name: Ally Financial
description: Former GMAC. Since December 2016 it has bought Carvana's auto loans under a master purchase agreement, recently committing up to $4B a year.

name: Wayfair
description: Founded in 2002 as CSN Stores by Niraj Shah and Steve Conine, Cornell roommates. Bootstrapped until 2011 and listed on the NYSE in October 2014. Class B shares carry ten votes.

name: Penske Corporation
description: Roger Penske's private holding company (1969), with interests in auto retail, truck leasing, logistics and motorsport, and 67% of Penske Entertainment (Fox holds 33%).

name: Penske Automotive Group
description: Began as United Auto Group (1990) and renamed in 2007. It sells brands including Toyota, Lexus, Honda and Mercedes-Benz and owns 28.9% of Penske Truck Leasing.

name: Penske Truck Leasing
description: Founded Dec 1, 1969. A GE Capital partnership from 1988, when GE contributed Gelco Truck Leasing; GE sold out in 2015–17. Owned 41.1% by Penske Corp., 28.9% by PAG and 30% by Mitsui.

name: Mitsui & Co.
description: Bought 20% of Penske Truck Leasing from GE Capital in 2015 for about $750M, then most of GE's last 15.5% in 2017.

name: Detroit Diesel
description: GM's diesel engine unit. Penske took 60% in 1988 and rebuilt its market share; it was sold to DaimlerChrysler in 2000.

name: General Motors
description: Detroit automaker. Roger Penske built his business on a Chevrolet dealership and took control of GM's Detroit Diesel unit in 1988.

name: Indianapolis Motor Speedway
description: Home of the Indianapolis 500. The Hulman family sold it and IndyCar to Penske on Nov 4, 2019; it is now held through Penske Entertainment.

name: D.R. Horton
description: Founded in 1978 in Fort Worth, listed in 1992 and the largest U.S. homebuilder by volume since 2002. Based in Arlington, Texas.

name: Forestar Group
description: D.R. Horton bought 75% of it for $558.3M in October 2017. A master supply agreement gives Horton first offer on its lots; Forestar is a NYSE 'controlled company'.

name: University of Oregon
description: Phil Knight's alma mater (1959), where Bill Bowerman coached him; Knight has given it over $2B.

name: Blue Origin
description: Bezos's privately held space company, founded in 2000 and funded by roughly $1B a year of his Amazon share sales. Forbes values it at about $130B.

name: The Washington Post
description: Bought by Jeff Bezos for $250M in 2013 through his holding company Nash Holdings.

name: LinkedIn
description: Founded in December 2002 by Reid Hoffman and former PayPal colleagues. Sequoia led its 2003 Series A, and Sequoia and Greylock joined a 2008 round at about $1B. Microsoft bought it for $26.2B, closing Dec 8, 2016.

name: Dell Technologies
description: Founded in 1984 as PC's Limited. It was taken private in 2013 with Silver Lake and a $2B Microsoft loan, bought EMC for $67B in 2016 and relisted in 2018. It builds Nvidia-based AI servers, including servers for xAI's Memphis supercomputer.

name: Silver Lake
description: Technology buyout firm that took Dell private with Michael Dell in 2013 for $24.4B. In June 2026 it still held 7.2% of Dell's stock and 13% of the votes.

name: Salesforce
description: Founded in March 1999 by ex-Oracle executive Marc Benioff and others, with seed money from Larry Ellison. It listed in 2004 and bought Tableau ($15.7B) and Slack ($27.7B).

name: Netflix
description: Founded in 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph, listed in 2002 and streaming since 2007. It paid Comcast for direct interconnection in 2014. In Feb 2026 it lost Warner Bros. Discovery to Paramount Skydance and received a $2.8B termination fee.

name: Block (Square)
description: Founded as Square in 2009 by Jack Dorsey and Jim McKelvey. It listed in 2015, was renamed Block in 2021, bought Afterpay for $29B and joined the S&P 500 in July 2025.

name: Paramount Skydance
description: Formed in August 2025 when David Ellison's Skydance merged with Paramount Global, financed by the Ellison family trust; Larry Ellison owns nearly 50%. In 2026 it outbid Netflix for Warner Bros. Discovery at $31 a share (over $110B including debt).

name: Cascade Investment
description: Bill Gates's private investment firm, founded in 1995 and run by Michael Larson. It holds 71% of Four Seasons, large stakes in Republic Services, Ecolab, Canadian National and Deere, and about 269,000 acres of U.S. farmland.

name: Chan Zuckerberg Initiative
description: Founded Dec 1, 2015 by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan as an LLC rather than a foundation, to receive 99% of their Facebook shares over their lifetimes. It funds the Biohub and science, education and housing work.

name: Energy Transfer
description: Founded in 1996 by Kelcy Warren and Ray Davis with about 200 miles of East Texas pipe. Through Sunoco, Southern Union, Regency and Crestwood it grew to about 130,000-140,000 miles. It owns 36.4% of Dakota Access.

name: Kinder Morgan
description: Formed in 1997 when Richard Kinder and William Morgan bought Enron Liquids Pipeline's general partner for $40M. It was taken private in 2007 and re-listed in 2011 (then the largest PE-backed US IPO), and grew to about 78,000 miles of pipeline.

name: Enron
description: Formed in 1985 by merging Houston Natural Gas and InterNorth into the second-largest US gas pipeline system. Richard Kinder was president from 1990 to 1996. It filed for bankruptcy on December 2, 2001, after accounting fraud.

name: Continental Resources
description: Founded in 1967 as Shelly Dean Oil and renamed in 1990. It opened up the North Dakota Bakken with horizontal fracked wells, listed in 2007, and was taken private by the Hamm family for $4.3B in 2022. (Fortune ranked it 503rd in 2025, just outside the 500.)

name: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals
description: Founded in 1988 by Leonard Schleifer and George Yancopoulos, IPO 1991. It makes Eylea, Dupixent and Libtayo, partnered with Sanofi from 2007, and has a dual-class structure with ten-vote Class A stock.

name: Universal Health Services
description: Founded by Alan B. Miller in King of Prussia in 1979 and listed in 1981. It runs acute-care hospitals and more than 300 behavioral-health facilities in the US and UK, and the Miller family controls it through super-voting Class C stock.

name: Tele-Communications Inc. (TCI)
description: Founded by Bob Magness in Denver in 1968, run by John Malone from 1973, and the largest US cable company by 1982. AT&T bought it in 1999 for $32B in stock plus $16B of debt, and it became AT&T Broadband.

name: Liberty Media
description: Spun out of TCI in 1991 and controlled by John Malone through Class B shares. It specializes in tax-free spinoffs and tracking stocks, owns Formula One (2017) and MotoGP (2025), and earlier co-owned QVC with Comcast and held 47.9% of DirecTV.

name: AT&T
description: Bought TCI in 1999 and turned its systems into AT&T Broadband, which it sold to Comcast in 2002. In 2025 it agreed to buy EchoStar spectrum for $23B.

name: EchoStar
description: Co-founded in 1980 by Charlie Ergen, Candy Ergen and Jim DeFranco. It created DISH Network (spun off in 2008, recombined in 2023) and sold spectrum to AT&T ($23B) and SpaceX (about $17B, half in stock) in 2025.

name: Career Communications Group
description: Baltimore-based private publisher founded by Tyrone Taborn in the mid-1980s. It publishes US Black Engineer & IT, Hispanic Engineer & IT and Women of Color, and runs the BEYA and Women of Color STEM conferences.

name: BEYA STEM Conference
description: The Black Engineer of the Year Awards, co-founded by Tyrone Taborn and Morgan State dean Eugene DeLoatch and first held at Morgan State in February 1987. It is co-hosted by CCG, the HBCU engineering deans and Lockheed Martin, and draws more than 10,000 attendees and 100+ recruiting companies.

name: Lockheed Martin
description: Long-time co-host of the BEYA STEM Conference, alongside CCG and the Council of Engineering Deans of the HBCUs.

name: Johns Hopkins University
description: Baltimore research university. John Malone earned an MS and a PhD in operations research there, and Tyrone Taborn holds a BS from it.
